posts.title: Tue 25 Aug, 18:30
posts.caption:
This is the part of an underfloor heating system nobody ever sees — and it's the part that decides whether it works properly.

That's a manifold. Every loop of pipe under the floor comes back to it, and each loop gets its own flow meter so the amount of water going round it can be set and balanced. Get that wrong and you end up with one warm room and one cold one, in a system that cost a lot of money to put in.

Two things worth knowing about underfloor:

🔥 It runs at a much lower water temperature than radiators. The floor is a huge surface area, so it doesn't need to be scalding to heat the room — which is also why it pairs well with a heat pump.

🏷️ Every circuit on this one is labelled. Sounds obvious. It isn't — plenty aren't, and the day something needs balancing or isolating, whoever's stood in front of it is guessing.

One practical thing if you've got it: underfloor is slower to react than radiators. It wants leaving on a steady setting rather than being flicked on and off like a radiator system.

Got underfloor in, or thinking about it? Which room? 👇

Sometime in October there'll be a first properly cold morning. Everybody puts the heating on the same weekend — and the boilers that have sat untouched all summer are the ones that don't come back on.

That's the whole reason September is worth using.

📅 You get a choice of dates. Book in autumn and you pick a morning that suits you. Leave it until the cold snap and you take whatever's left, behind everyone else who had the same idea on the same day.

🔍 Anything found is a planned job, not an emergency. A part ordered in September gets ordered while the heating still isn't needed. The same part ordered in November gets ordered while you're sat in the cold waiting for it.

📄 And the guarantee doesn't wait for the weather. Most makers tie it to a service every twelve months from the install date — so the month it's due is the month it's due, whether or not the heating's been on.

None of that is a hard sell — book it with whoever you like. Just don't leave it until the house is cold.

posts.caption:
See the black cylinder on the pipework under the boiler? That's a magnetic filter.

We talked last week about the black sludge that collects in the bottom of radiators and stops them heating properly. This is the thing that gets it out — so here's the other half of that story.

One line of recap: steel radiators and steel pipework shed rust into the water they're full of, and it ends up settling exactly where you don't want it. The copper you can see in this photo is fine — copper doesn't rust. It's the steel everywhere else in the system that's shedding.

What the filter does about it is simple. There's a magnet down the middle of it. Water passes through, the debris sticks to the magnet, and it stops going round and round the system.

Two things people don't realise:

🧲 It doesn't look after itself. It fills up, and it has to be opened and cleaned out before it'll catch anything else. Ask whoever services your boiler whether they do it — it isn't automatically part of a gas service, and it's worth knowing either way.

📄 Plenty of boiler guarantees expect one to be fitted and the system properly cleaned when a new boiler goes on. Worth reading what yours actually says.

🛑 Not one for a weekend. Cleaning a filter out means isolating it and draining hot, dirty system water off at the boiler. Get it wrong and it's a soaked floor at best. Leave it to whoever services the boiler.

If you've had a boiler fitted and there's nothing like this on the pipework, that's a fair question to ask.

Anyone had theirs opened up and seen what comes out? 👇

Most people who follow this page know us for boilers. This is a bathroom we finished in Bolton — bathrooms are a big part of what we do.

The bit worth pointing at is the lit niche in the tiling. It's a recess built into the wall while the wall is being built, with a light strip in it. On a job that's already happening it adds very little, and you get somewhere to put the shampoo that isn't a plastic rack hanging off the shower screen — plus a soft light in the evening the ceiling light can't do.

Here's the point though. It's a decision you can only make once. A niche goes in before the tiling. Afterwards it's a rip-out.

Same goes for everything that lives behind the wall — where the shower valve sits, how high the towel rail goes, where the extractor ducts to, whether there's a socket for a shaver. All of it is easy at the drawing stage and expensive halfway through.

So if you're planning one: spend the time before anything gets ordered, not after.

posts.caption:
MYTH: "It's cheaper to leave the heating on low all day than to keep turning it on and off."

This one gets argued about every winter, usually in a Facebook group, usually by two people who are both completely certain.

Here's the plain version. A house leaks heat to the outside all the time, and the warmer it is inside compared to out, the faster it leaks. Keep the place warm for twenty-four hours and you've paid to replace that leak for twenty-four hours. Heat it for the hours you're actually in and awake, and there are hours where you're not paying for it at all.

So for the vast majority of homes, a timer set to suit how you actually live beats leaving it ticking over. If you'd rather read it somewhere that isn't a plumber's Facebook page, the Energy Saving Trust is a good independent place to start: https://energysavingtrust.org.uk/

The honest caveat, because it isn't a religion: if a house is very poorly insulated, or somebody's home all day, or the system is underfloor and slow to react, the sums get closer together.

And the bigger saving isn't the argument at all — it's the controls. A thermostat that works, a timer set to real life, and radiator valves turned down in rooms nobody sits in will beat either approach.

Which camp are you in? 👇

posts.caption:
New boiler, new pipework, and — the part that actually changes what you spend — new controls.

People spend weeks choosing a boiler and about four minutes choosing what tells it when to run. It's the wrong way round. A modern boiler wired to a thirty-year-old timer and a dial in the hall can't do most of what it was built to do.

What decent controls give you:

🌡️ A room thermostat that talks to the boiler properly, so it can run cooler and longer instead of firing flat out and stopping. Boilers are at their most efficient when they're ticking along gently, not when they're roaring.

⏱️ A timer that matches how the house is actually used — rather than whatever it was left on by the people who lived there before.

🚪 Radiator valves set room by room, so the spare bedroom isn't being heated to the same temperature as the room you're sat in.

None of it is glamorous and none of it gets advertised. It's still the cheapest real improvement available to most heating systems in Bolton.

🛑 One for a professional, not a weekend. Changing the batteries in a wireless thermostat, fine. Anything behind a faceplate is electrical work wired into a heating system — that wants a competent heating engineer or an electrician, and anything touching the gas appliance itself wants a Gas Safe registered engineer. Not a screwdriver and a video.

What are you running yours on — a dial on the wall, or an app? 👇

posts.caption:
A walk-in shower, finished in Bolton. Worth saying what's underneath one of these — because the tiling is the part everyone looks at, and the part that goes wrong is never the tiling.

Three things decide whether a walk-in lasts:

1️⃣ The fall of the floor. Water has to run to the drain on its own. A few millimetres out over a metre and you've got a puddle that sits there every single day for the next fifteen years.

2️⃣ The tanking. That's the waterproof layer bonded to the floor and up the walls before a single tile goes on. You will never see it. If it isn't there, or it's been rushed, you find out about it through the ceiling below.

3️⃣ The waste and the flow rate. A big rainfall head puts out a lot of water and it has to get away as fast as it arrives. That's a question about pipework, not about the shower head.

None of that shows up in a photograph — which is exactly why it's worth asking about when you're comparing quotes. Anyone who's done it properly will be pleased you asked.

Bath or shower — which way would you go if you were doing yours? 👇

posts.title: Mon 31 Aug, 09:45
posts.caption:
Heating not coming on? Four things worth checking before you ring anybody. They take two minutes and they sort it more often than you'd think.

1️⃣ Is anything actually asking for heat? Check the programmer is on and in the right mode, and that the room thermostat is set higher than the room already is. If the house is 21 and the stat says 19, the boiler is doing exactly what it's been told.

2️⃣ Look at the pressure gauge on the front of the boiler. Most want somewhere around 1 to 1.5 bar with the system cold. Drop below that and a lot of boilers simply refuse to fire.

3️⃣ Check the batteries in the wireless thermostat. Not a joke — it is one of the most common causes of "the heating's dead" there is.

4️⃣ Check the switch and the fuse. There's usually a fused spur on the wall near the boiler, and it gets knocked off during decorating far more often than anyone admits.

🛑 Where to stop. If there's a fault code on the display, if it keeps losing pressure, if there's water anywhere there shouldn't be, or if you can smell gas — stop there and get a Gas Safe registered engineer out. Nothing behind the boiler's case is a DIY job.

And if you can smell gas, that's 0800 111 999 first and everything else after.

You can check any engineer's registration free in about thirty seconds here: https://www.gassaferegister.co.uk

Which of those four has caught you out before? 👇

posts.caption:
A boiler in a cellar, and the reason this one needed more thought than usual.

Every boiler fitted these days is a condensing boiler, and when it's running cool enough it does what the name says: the flue gases are cooled far enough that the moisture in them turns back into liquid water instead of going up the flue as vapour. Recovering that heat is exactly why they're efficient — and it's also why the cooler you can run a system, the better it works.

That water has to go somewhere. Normally it runs off to a drain by gravity, because the boiler sits above the drain.

In a cellar it doesn't. There's nothing downhill to run to. So this one has a condensate pump: the water collects in a small tank, and when it reaches a level the pump lifts it up and out to where it can drain away properly.

Two things worth knowing if you've got one:

⚡ It's an electrical item with moving parts, so unlike a plain plastic pipe it can fail. If it does, the boiler will normally lock out rather than let water go on the floor. That's it doing its job, not breaking.

🧊 The length of condensate pipe that runs outside is the bit that freezes in a hard frost and stops the boiler dead. On an exposed run it wants insulating, and in the wider pipe size rather than the narrow one. Worth sorting in September, not January.

Cellars, lofts, cupboards you can barely get an arm into — awkward spaces are most of the job in older Bolton housing.

Where's yours? Kitchen, loft, cellar, or somewhere daft? 👇

posts.caption:
The numbers on a radiator valve are not a temperature, and they're not a volume dial either. Almost everyone assumes one or the other.

That white knob with 1 to 5 on it is a TRV — a thermostatic radiator valve. Inside it is a small element that expands as the air around it warms, and as it expands it closes the valve down. So it isn't setting how hot the radiator gets. It's setting how warm the room is allowed to get before that radiator shuts itself off.

Which means:

🔢 Turning it up to 5 doesn't warm the room any faster. It just lets the room get hotter before the radiator stops. Same as the thermostat myth — it's a target, not an accelerator.

🛏️ Different rooms want different numbers. A bedroom on 2 or 3 and a living room on 4 is a perfectly sensible house. Heating a spare room nobody uses to the same temperature as the room you're sat in is money going straight out through the wall.

🚫 On many systems one radiator has no TRV on it by design — usually the one in the same room as the main thermostat. That's deliberate. The system needs somewhere for water to go when everything else has closed down. Don't let anyone fit one there without checking.

🛑 One to leave alone: if a radiator's cold and the valve head won't turn, the pin underneath it has usually seized. That's an engineer's job rather than a screwdriver and hope — force it and the system can end up on your carpet.

Go and look at the one in the room you're sat in. What number is it on? 👇
